p: Chagatai was born in late 1183 or 1184 to Börte, of the Onggirat tribe, and Temüjin, the later Genghis Khan. Because Börte had been kidnapped by the Merkit tribe before the birth of her elder son Jochi, whose paternity was never known, Chagatai was the first son definitively fathered by Temüjin. When Genghis divided his new nation after the assembly of 1206, Chagatai received territories near the Altai Mountains and either 4,000 or 8,000 subjects. He was known for his knowledge of Mongol law and custom, and chroniclers such as Juzjani noted the harshness of his temperament.

With his brothers Jochi and Ögedei he commanded the right wing in the invasion of the Jin dynasty in 1211. In the invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire in 1219 he was charged with building bridges and maintaining roads. He and Ögedei besieged Otrar, which fell in February 1220; the Mongols killed or enslaved its entire population. At the Siege of Gurganj, which fell in April 1221, the usual narrative has Chagatai and Jochi quarrel over how to conduct it until Genghis placed Ögedei over both; the historian Christopher Atwood argues that this account was a later invention meant to support Ögedei's right to rule.

Genghis thought Chagatai too strict and narrow-minded for a ruler and was troubled by his hatred of Jochi, and excluded him from the succession. After Genghis died in 1227, Chagatai held to his father's will, prevented any usurpation before the accession of Ögedei in 1229, and presided over the coronation with Tolui and their uncle Temüge. In Central Asia his capital and summer pastures were at Almaliq. He disputed jurisdiction with the imperial official Mahmud Yalavach, and when Bukhara revolted against tax demands in 1238 he left its suppression to Ögedei's armies.

After Ögedei died in December 1241, Chagatai's support made Töregene regent. He died in 1242; his wife Yesülün accused a steward named Vajir of poisoning him and had him executed. His grandson Qara Hülegü succeeded him but was displaced by Chagatai's son Yesü-Möngke between 1246 and 1250.

Chagatai upheld traditional Mongol law, which forbade elements of Islamic practice, and gained a reputation for being anti-Muslim; one contemporary Muslim writer claimed that he urged Ögedei to kill every Muslim in the empire. The historians Michael Hope and Peter Jackson think this far from the truth, pointing to the powerful Muslim officials at his court. His descendants were nonetheless far slower to convert to Islam than the rulers of the Golden Horde and the Ilkhanate.

notes: The existing entry dates his rule 'r. 1227-1242'; the article says he was granted the Central Asian lands 'after the conclusion of the Khwarazmian campaign' without a year. I gave no start date.
The article spells the son both 'Yesu-Mongke' and 'Yesü-Möngke'; I used the latter.
Left out the anecdote of Mutukan's death and the drinking-cup story for length.
